student_profile.student_background: Practicing healthcare professionals across roles — clinicians, nurses, allied health staff, administrators, and researchers — non-technical, no programming assumed. The audience spans the three levels of the organization's AI taxonomy, and a single course serves all three: Operators (limited end-user interaction with the AI; need to accurately interpret outputs and ensure the technology enhances rather than replaces judgement); Contributors (interact with the AI but do not make decisions about the technology); and Shapers (interact with the AI and hold decision-making capacity).
student_profile.aggregate_academic_performance: Experienced adult professionals with strong domain readiness; mixed comfort and confidence with AI tools, ranging from enthusiastic early adopters to cautious skeptics.
student_profile.anticipated_learner_needs_and_barriers: Wide variation in AI fluency and confidence; assume little to no formal AI training and some anxiety or skepticism. Learners benefit from plain language, concrete but generic clinical examples, jargon defined on first use, and an explicitly judgment-free space to ask questions. Time-constrained; the course is delivered as short daily sessions and should be applied and awareness-focused rather than technical.

instructor_preferences.instructor_emphasis_intent: This is a generic AWARENESS course on the PROS AND CONS of using AI in healthcare. It must be STRICTLY TOOL-AGNOSTIC: never name any vendor, company, or commercial product (no brand names of any kind — this avoids permission and approval issues with medical schools); teach generic AI-assistant and AI-system skills that apply to any tool of that category. When a real-world failure or success story is instructive, describe it generically (for example ``an early oncology decision-support system whose recommendations proved inconsistent'' or ``a widely deployed sepsis prediction model with low real-world sensitivity'') without naming the product or company. For every case, cover both the benefits (pros) and the risks and limitations (cons), and give substantive treatment to ALL FOUR core concepts in EVERY case: safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability. Ground the framing in public regulatory material — the FDA's Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) and AI-enabled-device resources, Good Machine Learning Practice, and transparency guiding principles — and use only publicly available examples and generic device categories, never a proprietary or institution-specific example. Examples never use patient-identifiable data. Because healthcare-AI guidelines are still emerging, emphasize building awareness and judgment over fixed rules.
instructor_preferences.instructor_style_preferences: Each module covers ONE AI use-case area with a clear arc: what the AI does in that area; the benefits (pros); the risks and limitations (cons); how safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability each apply; and what the Operator, the Contributor, and the Shaper each need to interpret, do, and decide — EVERY module must explicitly address all three roles, including the research module. Make slides substantive and dense: each content slide carries 4-6 full teaching bullets that fill the slide — a slide with only 1-2 short bullets and large empty space is a defect. Use visual structure where it teaches better than prose: two-column pros/cons tables, a three-role responsibility grid per case, and comparison tables. Make the course interactive: in each session block include a discussion prompt slide, a decision-point scenario slide (``the AI suggests X — accept, verify, or escalate?''), and a short knowledge-check slide with 2-3 questions. Keep language plain, define every term on first use, and never name specific commercial tools or products.
instructor_preferences.instructor_focus_for_assessment: Assess judgment and awareness — the ability to weigh the pros and cons of AI in an area, apply safety/trustworthiness/validation/explainability, and decide when to trust or question an AI output — rather than technical skill. No exams or coding.

course_structure.course_learning_outcomes: For each major area of AI use in medicine — clinical documentation, medical imaging, diagnosis and decision support, health-data management, and scientific research — explain in plain language how the AI is used and weigh its benefits against its risks and limitations; apply the core concepts of safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability to judge whether and how far to trust an AI output; keep clinical judgment central and recognize where AI should not replace it; and understand what each role — Operator, Contributor, Shaper — needs to know and decide in every area. This is an awareness course on the pros and cons of AI in healthcare, not training on any specific product or tool.
course_structure.total_number_of_weeks: 5 cases (each delivered over roughly 5-6 one-hour sessions)
course_structure.weekly_schedule_outline:
AI-Driven Clinical Documentation (note-taking): how AI drafts clinical notes and its benefits — less documentation burden, more patient time, consistency — versus the risks: omissions and hallucinations (for example a missed medication allergy), accountability for the signed note, and recording privacy; safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability each applied to documentation; what the Operator, Contributor, and Shaper each must watch for and decide
AI in Medical Imaging (image analysis and image-to-text reports): how AI triages and reads scans and drafts reports — the benefits of speed and catching subtle findings — versus the risks: missed or false findings, poor generalization across scanners and populations, and over-trusting a draft report; safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability each applied to imaging AI; the Operator reading flagged results, the Contributor incorporating them, and the Shaper evaluating the tool category
AI for Diagnosis and Clinical Decision Support: how AI supports diagnosis and clinical decisions — earlier detection and help on complex cases — versus the risks: automation bias, false positives and negatives, opaque reasoning, and alert fatigue; keeping clinician judgment central; safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability each applied to decision support; the Operator interpreting suggestions, the Contributor using them in workflow, and the Shaper adopting and governing them
AI-Driven Health Data Management: how AI organizes, retrieves, and summarizes health data — faster access and surfacing relevant history — versus the risks: privacy and protected-health-information exposure, biased or incomplete summaries, and poor data quality; safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability each applied to data management; the Operator using summaries, the Contributor relying on retrieval, and the Shaper governing data access and vendor choices
AI in Scientific and Clinical Research: how AI accelerates research — literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, drug discovery, and trial matching — versus the risks: fabricated citations, reproducibility problems, training-data bias, and over-claiming; safety, trustworthiness, validation, and explainability each applied to research use; the Operator reading AI-assisted findings critically, the Contributor using AI in research workflows, and the Shaper setting standards for AI-assisted studies

assessment_design.assessment_format_preferences: No exams and no coding. Pros-and-Cons Analysis (35%) — for an assigned AI use-case area, lay out the benefits and the risks and judge when the AI should be trusted or questioned. Reflection (25%) — connect each area to the learner's own role and practice. Scenario Judgment (25%) — work a short, generic clinical scenario and apply safety/trustworthiness/validation/explainability. Participation (15%) — engage in the discussion prompts and decision-point scenarios, modeling openness to questions. Emphasis on judgment and awareness over technical output.
assessment_design.assessment_delivery_constraints: Submissions via the organization's learning platform in standard formats; deliverables are short and applied to suit busy clinical professionals across short daily sessions.

teaching_constraints.platform_policy_constraints: Hosted on an institution-approved learning platform; materials must meet accessibility standards and clinical privacy expectations — examples must never include patient-identifiable information, and content must stay strictly tool-agnostic (no vendor, company, or product names).
teaching_constraints.ta_support_availability: Facilitator-led or self-paced; small-group discussion support where available; no teaching assistant or grading staff assumed.
teaching_constraints.instructional_delivery_context: Professional development for working clinical teams, delivered as short daily sessions of about one hour, with each of the five cases spanning roughly five to six sessions; built around discussion prompts, decision-point scenarios, pros-and-cons analysis, and knowledge checks rather than laboratory or coding activities.

institutional_requirements.program_learning_outcomes: Aligns with the digital-education program's goals for responsible, inclusive AI adoption and effective judgment about AI in clinical settings.
institutional_requirements.academic_policies_and_institutional_stan: Adheres to healthcare-organization policies on accessibility, privacy, and responsible AI use; all examples avoid patient-identifiable information, stay strictly tool-agnostic, and reflect clinical-ethics norms. Framing draws on public regulatory material (FDA SaMD and AI-enabled-device resources) rather than institution-specific rules.
institutional_requirements.department_syllabus_requirements: Required components include learning outcomes, a case-by-case schedule, the assessment approach, and an explicit statement that the course builds awareness of the pros and cons of AI and does not endorse any specific product.

prior_feedback.historical_course_evaluation_results: First revision. Feedback on the previous draft: specific vendor and product names appeared despite the tool-agnostic requirement (must be fully generic); the research module omitted the three roles (every module must address Operator, Contributor, and Shaper); the four core concepts were unevenly covered across modules (each module must treat all four substantively); and many slides were sparse (1-2 bullets with large empty space) and lacked interactive elements — slides must be dense and each session block needs discussion, decision-point, and knowledge-check moments.
